question_text: A GenAI application generates daily personalised reports. Users complain about long wait times before seeing any content. Which TWO approaches most reduce perceived latency?

options.text: Enable response streaming so users see text incrementally as the FM generates it
Pre-compute reports overnight when query patterns are predictable and cache the results
Increase Lambda memory allocation to maximum (10GB)
Use a larger FM to reduce the number of tokens generated
Increase the max output token limit to generate more complete responses

explanation: Skill 4.2.1 cites response streaming for immediate feedback and pre-computation for predictable queries. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte dramatically — users see content immediately rather than waiting for the full response. Pre-computation generates reports before the user requests them, making retrieval instant. Lambda memory affects cold-start and CPU allocation — but the bottleneck is FM inference, not Lambda compute. Larger FMs generate tokens slower per token. More tokens increases total latency.
source_topic: Response streaming, pre-computation, latency optimisation

question_text: A RAG system retrieves documents from OpenSearch but p99 retrieval latency is 800ms, exceeding the 300ms target. Which approaches specifically address retrieval latency? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Optimise OpenSearch index settings — tune HNSW parameters (ef_search, m) for the latency/recall tradeoff
Apply query preprocessing — normalise embeddings and filter on metadata before the ANN search to reduce the candidate set
Increase the FM context window to reduce the number of retrieval calls
Use a larger embedding model to improve result quality
Store vectors in Amazon Glacier for cost efficiency

explanation: Skill 4.2.2 describes index optimisation and query preprocessing for enhanced retrieval performance. (A) HNSW ef_search controls the ANN search graph traversal depth — lowering it reduces latency at a small recall cost. (B) Metadata pre-filtering narrows the ANN search space before vector comparison, reducing compute. Context window has no effect on retrieval latency. A larger embedding model is slower to embed — may worsen latency. Glacier has hours-long retrieval times — completely unsuitable for real-time RAG.
source_topic: OpenSearch index optimisation, HNSW, retrieval latency

question_text: A code generation assistant often produces creative but incorrect code. A factual Q&A assistant produces overly conservative, repetitive answers. What parameter adjustments address each issue?

options.text: Increase temperature for both applications
Code assistant: lower temperature (0.1–0.3) for deterministic output; Q&A assistant: slightly higher temperature (0.5–0.7) with diverse beam search to vary responses
Set temperature to 1.0 for all applications as a universal default
Reduce maxTokens for both applications to force conciseness

explanation: Skill 4.2.4 describes appropriate temperature and top-k/top-p selection based on requirements. For deterministic tasks (code generation), low temperature (0.1–0.3) reduces randomness and produces consistent correct code. For creative/diverse tasks (varied Q&A), moderate temperature (0.5–0.7) plus top-p/top-k sampling increases variety. A universal temperature of 1.0 ignores task requirements. Reducing maxTokens constrains output length but doesn't affect creativity or determinism.
source_topic: Temperature, top-k, top-p, FM inference parameters

question_text: A GenAI pipeline must retrieve data from 3 independent knowledge bases and combine the results before generation. Sequential retrieval takes 900ms total. How can this be reduced to ~300ms?

options.text: Call all three knowledge bases sequentially and optimise each call
Execute all three retrieval calls in parallel (e.g., Promise.all in Node.js or concurrent Futures in Python) and merge results
Use a single larger knowledge base to replace the three separate ones
Remove two of the three knowledge bases to reduce complexity

explanation: Skill 4.2.1 describes parallel requests for complex workflows to improve latency. If the three retrievals are independent, running them concurrently (Promise.all, asyncio.gather, or Step Functions parallel branches) reduces wall-clock time from the sum of all calls to approximately the time of the slowest single call — from 900ms to ~300ms. Sequential calls cannot achieve this. Merging knowledge bases changes the data architecture, not the call pattern. Removing knowledge bases loses coverage.
source_topic: Parallel FM requests, latency optimisation, async

question_text: A GenAI application experiences traffic spikes of 10x during weekday business hours and near-zero usage overnight. Which approach correctly handles this for a SageMaker-hosted model?

options.text: Provision peak capacity permanently to never fail
Configure SageMaker endpoint auto-scaling with a target tracking policy on InvocationsPerInstance, scaling in/out based on actual traffic
Use a fixed instance count of 2 and throttle requests above that capacity
Deploy a new endpoint every morning and delete it every evening manually

explanation: Skill 4.2.5 describes auto-scaling configurations optimised for GenAI traffic patterns. SageMaker Application Auto Scaling with InvocationsPerInstance target tracking automatically scales out during business-hour spikes and scales in overnight — balancing cost and capacity. Permanent peak capacity wastes cost overnight. A fixed 2-instance count throttles during spikes. Manual endpoint creation/deletion is error-prone and has deployment lead time.
source_topic: SageMaker auto-scaling, GenAI traffic, capacity planning

topic: SageMaker Model Monitor for drift detection
question_text: A fraud detection model deployed on a SageMaker endpoint was accurate at launch. Six months later, it is flagging far fewer fraudulent transactions. The team suspects the real-world data distribution has shifted since training. Which service alerts them to this drift automatically?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon CloudTrail
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines

explanation: SageMaker Model Monitor (Skill 4.2 — optimise application performance) continuously monitors model inputs and outputs in production, comparing real-world distributions against the training baseline and raising CloudWatch alarms when data drift exceeds configured thresholds. SageMaker Clarify (A) diagnoses the root cause of bias and explains model decisions (the 'why') — it is typically run as part of the investigation after Monitor alerts. CloudTrail tracks API calls. SageMaker Pipelines automates the retraining workflow — triggered by Monitor alarms but not responsible for detecting drift.
source_topic: SageMaker Model Monitor, data drift detection

question_text: After SageMaker Model Monitor fires a drift alarm, a data scientist needs to understand whether a specific feature (customer age group) is creating biased predictions. Which service provides feature-level explanations and bias metrics?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker Clarify — produces SHAP values and DPL bias metrics per feature
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines evaluation step

explanation: SageMaker Clarify (Skill 3.4.2, fairness evaluations) computes Shapley Values (SHAP) to quantify each feature's contribution to predictions, and Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL) to measure bias across sensitive groups (e.g. age). This is the 'root cause' tool. Model Monitor detects that something is wrong (drift symptom) — the canonical pair. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data. SageMaker Pipelines automates the workflow but does not itself produce SHAP/DPL analysis.
source_topic: SageMaker Clarify, SHAP, DPL, bias detection

topic: SageMaker model compression — quantization, pruning, distillation
question_text: A team needs to deploy an FM for real-time inference on resource-constrained hardware. They want to reduce the model's memory footprint and inference latency while retaining acceptable accuracy. Which THREE model compression techniques are applicable? (Select TWO)

options.text: Quantization — reduce the numerical precision of model weights (e.g. FP32 → INT8)
Knowledge distillation — train a smaller student model to mimic the larger teacher model
Increasing batch size — send more requests per second to the same model
Adding more transformer layers to improve accuracy before deployment
Pruning — remove low-importance weights from the model

explanation: Quantization reduces weight precision (FP32→INT8/FP16) dramatically cutting memory and speeding up inference. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller, faster student model using outputs from a larger teacher model. Both are standard compression strategies. Increasing batch size improves throughput but not per-request latency or memory footprint. Adding layers increases model size — the opposite of compression. Pruning (E) is also a valid compression technique, but the question asks for two answers and quantization + distillation are the most commonly tested on AIP-C01.
source_topic: Model compression, quantization, distillation, SageMaker Neo

question_text: A chatbot shows a blank screen for 4-5 seconds before displaying a response, making it feel slow even though the total response time is acceptable. What optimisation most directly improves PERCEIVED latency?

options.text: Switch to a faster model with lower total latency
Implement response streaming using InvokeModelWithResponseStream — display tokens as they are generated
Pre-compute all possible responses and cache them
Increase Lambda memory for faster processing

explanation: Streaming (InvokeModelWithResponseStream) delivers tokens to the UI as they are generated, eliminating the blank-screen wait. Users see content almost immediately (time-to-first-token < 500ms), making the interaction feel responsive even if total generation time is the same. Switching models reduces absolute latency but the blank-screen problem persists if streaming isn't used. Pre-computing requires knowing all queries in advance. Lambda memory doesn't affect FM generation speed.
source_topic: Response streaming to improve perceived chatbot latency

question_text: A daily reporting application generates the same set of 50 summary reports every morning at 9 AM. Users check these reports between 9 AM and 5 PM. Currently, each report is generated on-demand when a user requests it (3-5 second wait). How can latency be eliminated for users?

options.text: Implement response streaming so users see partial reports faster
Pre-compute all 50 reports at 8 AM via a Step Functions scheduled workflow, store results in DynamoDB — users retrieve instantly
Use Bedrock Provisioned Throughput to make on-demand generation faster
Increase the Lambda timeout to allow 10-second generation time

explanation: For predictable, recurring reports, pre-computation eliminates user-facing latency entirely: a Step Functions workflow runs at 8 AM, generates all reports via Bedrock, and stores them in DynamoDB. Users read from DynamoDB instantly (<10ms). Streaming still has generation latency. Provisioned Throughput reduces throttling risk but not individual request latency for complex generations. Lambda timeout extension doesn't help users waiting for on-demand generation.
source_topic: Pre-computation of predictable reports to eliminate user-facing latency

question_text: A document analysis pipeline processes 5 sections of a long document sequentially — each Bedrock call takes 3 seconds, totalling 15 seconds end-to-end. The sections are independent and can be processed in any order. What optimisation reduces total processing time?

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window to process all 5 sections in one call
Use Step Functions Map state or Lambda async invocations to process all 5 sections in parallel — reducing total time to ~3 seconds
Increase Lambda memory to speed up each individual section
Use Bedrock Batch Inference for real-time parallel processing

explanation: Since sections are independent, parallelisation is optimal. Using Step Functions Map state or async Lambda invocations launches all 5 Bedrock calls simultaneously, reducing wall-clock time from 15 seconds to ~3 seconds (the time of the slowest single call). A larger context window processes all sections in one call but may reduce quality (less focused analysis per section) and increases per-call cost. Lambda memory affects CPU-bound code, not external API call time. Batch Inference is async, not real-time.
source_topic: Step Functions Map state for parallel FM calls

question_text: A team is self-hosting a 70B-parameter open-source LLM on SageMaker. Inference latency is high due to model loading time and large model size. Which TWO model optimisation techniques directly reduce inference latency for self-hosted models?

options.text: Model quantisation — reduce weight precision from FP32 to FP16/INT8 to decrease model size and memory bandwidth requirements
Model pruning — remove unimportant weights to reduce model size and inference FLOPs
Fine-tuning the model on domain data
Increasing the Lambda function memory limit
Switching from SageMaker Batch Transform to real-time endpoints

explanation: Quantisation (A) reduces weight precision from FP32 to FP16 or INT8, halving or quartering memory bandwidth requirements — significantly reducing load time and inference latency on GPU. Pruning (B) removes weights that contribute little to model output, reducing the effective model size and FLOPs needed per inference. Fine-tuning (C) adapts the model but doesn't reduce its size. Lambda memory (D) is irrelevant for SageMaker-hosted models. Endpoint type (E) affects throughput pattern, not individual call latency.
source_topic: Model quantisation and pruning for self-hosted LLM latency reduction

question_text: A RAG system using OpenSearch has retrieval latency of 800ms for vector searches on a 100M embedding index. The team needs to reduce this below 200ms. Which OpenSearch-specific optimisations should they apply?

options.text: Apply metadata filters to narrow the candidate vector set BEFORE running ANN search
Tune HNSW parameters: increase ef_construction (better index quality at build time) and tune ef_search (controls recall-latency trade-off at query time)
Increase the embedding vector dimensionality from 1024 to 4096
Switch from HNSW to exact nearest-neighbour search for higher accuracy
Add more shards to distribute the index across nodes for parallel search execution

explanation: (A) Pre-filtering by metadata reduces the candidate vector space before ANN search, significantly reducing search time. (B) HNSW ef_search directly trades recall for speed — lowering ef_search reduces the search graph traversal depth, cutting latency at a small recall cost. Higher ef_construction improves index quality during build. Increasing dimensionality (C) increases memory and computation — opposite of what's needed. Exact NN (D) is dramatically slower than ANN. More shards (E) help throughput, not per-query latency for a single query.
source_topic: OpenSearch HNSW tuning + metadata pre-filtering for latency

topic: SageMaker model compression — quantization, pruning, distillation
question_text: A company wants to deploy a large 65B-parameter model on smaller, cheaper GPU instances to reduce inference costs. They are willing to accept a small quality degradation. Which technique creates a smaller, faster model that approximates the large model's behaviour?

options.text: Fine-tuning the large model on domain data
Knowledge distillation — train a smaller 'student' model to mimic the large 'teacher' model's outputs
Adding more training data to the large model
Enabling prompt caching on the large model

explanation: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller 'student' model by having it learn to match the large 'teacher' model's output distribution — producing a compact model that approximates the teacher's quality at a fraction of the compute cost. Fine-tuning adapts the existing model but doesn't reduce its size. More training data makes the large model better, not smaller. Prompt caching reduces redundant token costs but doesn't change model size or GPU requirements.
source_topic: Knowledge distillation for smaller, deployable FM

question_text: A team wants to compare two prompt variants against each other — measuring which produces higher user satisfaction scores and lower hallucination rates across 1,000 test queries. Which Bedrock tooling supports this systematic comparison?

options.text: Bedrock Prompt Flows — visual orchestration tool
Bedrock Prompt Management (to version both prompts) + Bedrock Model Evaluations (to run automated comparison with LLM-as-judge scoring)
Amazon CloudWatch A/B Metrics dashboard
AWS Step Functions comparing both prompts sequentially

explanation: Bedrock Prompt Management versions both prompt variants. Bedrock Model Evaluations then runs both against a 1,000-query test dataset, uses LLM-as-judge to score factual accuracy/hallucination rate, and produces a comparison report. This is the fully managed Bedrock evaluation pipeline. Prompt Flows orchestrates workflows, not evaluations. CloudWatch doesn't have A/B evaluation capabilities for prompt quality. Step Functions can run both prompts but doesn't provide automated quality scoring.
source_topic: Bedrock Prompt Management + Model Evaluations for prompt A/B testing

question_text: A company wants to continuously monitor their production RAG chatbot for hallucination rate — detecting when the model starts producing responses not supported by retrieved source documents. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Monitor ModelLatency in CloudWatch — high latency indicates hallucinations

Deploy a Lambda evaluation function that uses Bedrock contextual grounding checks or an LLM-as-judge to score each production response against retrieved chunks; publish hallucination_rate as a CloudWatch custom metric
Use Amazon Macie to detect hallucinated content in S3
Use AWS Config to check if Bedrock Guardrails are enabled

explanation: Hallucination rate is an AI-specific metric that requires ML-based evaluation: a Lambda function evaluates each response using Bedrock contextual grounding checks or an LLM-as-judge prompt ('Is this response supported by the provided context? Score 0-1'). The score is published to CloudWatch as a custom metric, enabling alarms when the rate exceeds threshold. Latency has no correlation with hallucination. Macie scans for sensitive data. Config monitors resource configurations.
source_topic: Production hallucination rate monitoring with CloudWatch custom metrics

topic: Tensor parallelism and GPU replica efficiency
question_text: A team hosting a 7B-parameter LLM on SageMaker finds that with tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs, inter-GPU communication overhead is eating 30% of inference time. The model actually fits on 2 GPUs. What is the BEST configuration change?

options.text: Increase tensor parallelism to 8 GPUs for more parallelism
Reduce tensor parallelism to 2 GPUs per model replica, and use the freed 2 GPUs for a second model replica — doubling throughput
Enable quantisation to reduce model size further
Move to a different instance type with fewer GPUs

explanation: Per the DJL tuning principle: 'Model fits on fewer GPUs → reduce tensor parallelism, increase replicas'. Reducing from 4 to 2 GPUs per replica eliminates the inter-GPU communication overhead on 2 extra GPUs, AND allows running 2 replicas on the same 4 GPUs — doubling throughput. Increasing to 8 GPUs (A) increases communication overhead further. Quantisation (C) helps memory/size but doesn't address the communication overhead. Changing instance type (D) doesn't solve the parallelism configuration.
source_topic: Reduce tensor parallelism, increase replicas for throughput

question_text: A team has a RAG application that also needs to join vector search results with structured user data stored in the same PostgreSQL database (e.g., filter results by user subscription tier stored in a relational table). Which vector store backend is BEST for this hybrid relational + vector search requirement?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless — best for pure vector workloads
Amazon MemoryDB — in-memory ultra-low latency
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector — SQL capabilities alongside vector similarity search in the same database
Amazon S3 Vectors — lowest cost option

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector enables SQL JOIN operations between vector search results and relational tables in the same query — exactly what's needed for filtering vectors by user subscription tier stored in a relational column. OpenSearch doesn't natively support SQL JOINs with relational tables. MemoryDB is in-memory with high cost and no relational capabilities. S3 Vectors is for cold, infrequent large-scale search, not real-time relational integration.
source_topic: Aurora pgvector for relational + vector hybrid queries

question_text: A company needs to process 50,000 product descriptions daily for embedding generation. The workload runs between midnight and 5 AM with no real-time user interaction. Which combination of Bedrock features minimises cost for this use case?

options.text: On-demand InvokeModel with maximum Lambda concurrency
Bedrock Batch Inference (StartBatchInferenceJob) reading from S3 — optimised for bulk async processing at lower effective cost
Bedrock Provisioned Throughput to guarantee batch throughput
SageMaker real-time endpoints with auto-scaling

explanation: Batch Inference is the cost-optimal choice for large-scale, non-real-time, offline processing: (1) it processes requests from S3 in bulk with lower overhead per item than synchronous calls, (2) there are no users waiting so the async nature is a benefit not a limitation, (3) it avoids the need for concurrent Lambda invocations or provisioned capacity. Provisioned Throughput adds an hourly commitment regardless of utilisation. SageMaker endpoints are for custom models and real-time serving.
source_topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for overnight bulk embedding generation

question_text: A latency-sensitive GenAI application needs to select the fastest Bedrock model for a given task. The team wants to regularly benchmark latency and throughput for their primary models. Where should they publish these benchmark results for ongoing analysis?

options.text: Store in a local CSV file on the developer's laptop
Publish to Amazon CloudWatch as custom metrics and build a dashboard comparing p50/p95/p99 latency across models
Log to an S3 bucket and review monthly
Use AWS Trusted Advisor latency recommendations

explanation: Publishing benchmark results to CloudWatch as custom metrics (ModelLatency by model_id) enables real-time dashboards, percentile statistics (p50/p95/p99), and alarms for regression detection. This supports data-driven model selection decisions. Local CSV files have no alarming or continuous collection. S3 + monthly review misses intra-month regressions. Trusted Advisor doesn't measure FM latency benchmarks.
source_topic: CloudWatch custom metrics for FM latency benchmarking
